bio.en: Teresa Torres is a product discovery coach and the author of Continuous Discovery Habits, who has helped thousands of product teams adopt a continuous discovery practice.
bio.zh: Teresa Torres 是一位产品发现（discovery）教练，也是《持续发现习惯》（Continuous Discovery Habits）一书的作者，她已帮助数千支产品团队建立起持续发现的工作方法。

summary.en: Teresa makes the case for continuous discovery: talking to customers every week and mapping opportunities and solutions with opportunity solution trees. She explains why discovery is a habit, not a one-off research phase, and how it keeps teams connected to real customer problems between releases. The episode is a practical, grounding guide to the product discovery practice every team can adopt.
summary.zh: Teresa 论证了“持续发现”的必要性：每周与客户交谈，并用“机会—解决方案树（opportunity solution trees）”来梳理机会与方案。她解释了为什么发现是一种习惯、而非一次性的研究阶段，以及它如何让团队在版本之间始终与真实的客户问题保持连接。本期是一份务实、扎根的指南，关于每支团队都能采纳的产品发现实践。

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah, that sounds great.
turns.zh: 是的，听起来很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So starting with the opportunity solution tree framework, it's such a simple but such a powerful way to visualize your strategy, your levers, how to prioritize, get buy-in from people, get everyone on the same page. It's probably the thing I share most of what you've put out with people. So I'd love to maybe start with just like what is this framework, what problem does it solve for people, and how can people apply it to their product problems?
turns.zh: 好的。那我们先从机会解决方案树框架开始吧。这是一个简单却强大的框架，用于可视化你的战略、杠杆、如何优先排序、获得人们的支持、让所有人达成共识。这可能是我与他人分享你发布的内容最多的部分了。所以我很想从这个框架是什么、它为人们解决什么问题，以及人们如何将其应用于产品问题开始。

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah, really good question. So first of all, it's just a really simple visual. It's funny how simple it looks, because using it in practice is really complex. I definitely have a new appreciation for that, trying to teach it over and over again and seeing where people struggle. (06:06): So it's a tree visual. So it's just like a decision tree. It starts with an outcome at the root of the tree, and then it branches into the opportunity space and then it branches into solutions, and maybe even assumption tests from there. (06:19): The purpose of it is I recognize that while as an industry, some companies are moving from this output focus to an outcome focus, most product teams don't really know how to manage this really complex problem of how do I start from an outcome and figure out what to build? It's a really unstructured, wide open, hard problem. (06:41): A lot of teams, they learn how to do their jobs building products by being told, "Build these features." That's a really structured, okay, I just turn out some work problem. And so, we're asking teams to fundamentally do a really different type of job and I think teams needed some scaffolding for how do you make that shift. And so, that was the purpose of the opportunity solution tree is how do I add some structure to this wide open, messy problem. (07:08): Now the reason why it looks simple but it's really hard in practice is like, well, what's an opportunity and how do I structure the opportunity space? I can tell you that opportunity is an unmet need pain point or desire, and that's great. But I can tell you that 98% of people that write opportunities write them as solutions. (07:26): So we tend to just really struggle with this distinction between the problem space and the solution space. I think that the heart of good product is really getting comfortable in the problem space or the opportunity space, really taking the time to frame a problem well, and to really get into what's needed before we jump to solutions. (07:48): But it's the opposite of how our brains are wired. And so, teaching people to be comfortable with that discomfort of staying there is hard. I mean I see blog posts written about how they're using the opportunity solution tree, and I cry a little bit because their opportunity space is all solutions. I don't want to knock down somebody's blog post, but I also don't want this bad example out there in the world when I'm trying to teach how do we do this well. So I haven't found the right line there yet other than I'm going to blog about good examples.
turns.zh: 是啊，这个问题问得真好。首先，这只是一个非常简单的视觉框架。说起来简单，却在实际应用中极其复杂。我在反复讲解这个方法时，越来越深刻地体会到这一点——每次看到学员们在理解关键点时卡壳，我都倍感挫败。（06:06）：这个树状框架其实就是决策树。它以树根处的结果为起点，向外延伸至机会空间，再分支到解决方案，甚至可能延伸至假设验证环节。（06:19）：它的核心在于，我发现虽然整个行业正从输出导向转向结果导向，但大多数产品团队仍无从下手如何从结果出发，规划产品路线。这是个极其开放、混乱且高难度的挑战。（06:41）：许多团队通过被动接受需求清单来完成产品开发——那是结构化的工作模式，简单粗暴。但我们要求团队从根本上转变思维模式，这就需要搭建清晰的框架。因此，机会解决方案树的意义在于为这个庞杂的开放性问题注入结构性。（07:08）：为什么看起来简单，实则难于实践？关键在于，什么是真正的机会？如何构建机会空间？我可以告诉你，机会是未被满足的需求、痛点或渴望，这固然不错。但令人遗憾的是，98%的团队在写机会描述时，都直接将其转化为解决方案。（07:26）：我们在区分问题空间与解决方案空间时往往陷入困境。优秀产品经理的核心能力在于，善于在问题空间中深挖，精准界定需求，再才去构思解决方案。（07:48）：但这与我们大脑的思维模式背道而驰。教会人们在这种不适中保持耐心实属不易。比如我看到有人分享使用机会解决方案树的博文时，总忍不住叹息——他们的机会空间全是解决方案。我无意贬低他人，但在传授正确方法时，实在不希望看到这种误解。所以目前我还在寻找平衡点——或许我该专门写一篇优质案例分享。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of a tree that, just to make it even more concrete, like for a company or product that you've worked with or that you think about?
turns.zh: 你能举个具体的树状框架示例吗？比如你曾参与或研究过的公司或产品？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah. So I like to use streaming entertainment as my examples, because literally everybody in the world is familiar with Netflix. If I think about their opportunity space, I recommend teams structure the opportunity space using an experience map, like if you take your outcome. (08:41): So if we start with Netflix, if you think about the experience of you're trying to get me to engage with Netflix more, I want to understand what's the experience of somebody using streaming entertainment to entertain themselves. Maybe even broader than Netflix. If you watch YouTube TV, that's probably still relevant for me to learn about and understand. (09:02): And so, the way that I'm going to structure my opportunity space is I'm going to look at what's the overall experience of trying to entertain yourself a streaming entertainment. That might look like, well, first there's this trigger of I need to decide to watch something. Then there's this experience of how am I deciding what to watch? Usually wrapped up in that is what platform am I watching it on? Those are sometimes inner mixed, because maybe you're deciding, "I want to watch Game of Thrones ," and that's right away sending you to HBO Max, or maybe you're like, "Well, I want to watch a movie," and I could be on any platform. (09:34): Then there's the evaluation process of is this movie good or not? Does it look like something I want to watch? Then I want to get into, okay, I'm ready to watch. Is it a good viewing experience? Then for a lot of these platforms, there's also this post-viewing experience of like am I going to encourage you to keep watching, things like that? (09:52): So that's how I would structure that opportunity space is just there's these distinct moments in time. Then what I'm capturing is, below each of those, what are the needs and pain points and desires that arise? So if we just focus on that one around how do I decide what to watch, there's all sorts of needs that come up. Some are really tactical, like I have a movie title in mind and I just don't know how to find it. That's a pain point. Or, hey, I was watching a show. How do I get back to it? It's also a pain point. But then there's also these big media opportunities, like I can't tell if this show is good or not. (10:27): And so, everything that I just said, there was no solutions in there. In fact, whether I work at Netflix or I work at Hulu, our opportunity spaces probably look pretty similar. Now the ones we choose to go after and how we solve them might look really different. But the core human needs of what's your experience as we go about our lives entertaining ourselves is pretty similar. (10:51): I think the companies that build really good products, they either intuitively or explicitly take the time to really understand what does that journey look like and what are those needs and pain points and how do we create a really seamless experience?
turns.zh: 是的。所以我喜欢用流媒体娱乐作为例子，因为世界上几乎每个人都熟悉Netflix。如果我思考他们的机会空间，我建议团队用体验地图来构建机会空间。比如，如果你以结果为出发点的话。（08:41）：那么以Netflix为例，如果你想让用户更多地使用Netflix娱乐，我想了解用户使用流媒体娱乐娱乐自己的体验是什么。甚至可能比Netflix更广泛。如果你看YouTube TV，这对我来说可能仍然有借鉴意义。（09:02）：所以我构建机会空间的方式是，我会观察尝试用流媒体娱乐娱乐自己的整体体验。可能首先是触发因素，我需要决定看什么。然后是如何决定看什么的体验？通常这与使用哪个平台相关。这些有时会相互交织，比如你可能决定看《权力的游戏》，这会直接把你导向HBO Max，或者你可能想看电影，但可以在任何平台上观看。（09:34）：然后是评估过程，这部电影好不好？看起来我想看吗？接下来是准备观看的体验，观看体验好吗？对于许多平台来说，还有观看后的体验，比如我们是否会鼓励用户继续观看之类的？（09:52）：所以我构建机会空间的方式就是，分出这些不同的时间点。然后我在每个时间点下方捕捉出现的需求、痛点和愿望。那么如果我们只关注如何决定看什么这一点，就会出现各种需求。有些是实际的，比如我心里有部电影的片名，但不知道怎么找到它。这就是痛点。或者，嘿，我之前在看一部剧，如何回到它那里？这也是痛点。但也有一些大的媒体机会，比如我不知道这部剧好不好。（10:27）：所以我刚才说的所有内容里，都没有解决方案。事实上，无论我在Netflix还是Hulu工作，我们的机会空间可能看起来很相似。现在我们选择追逐的那些机会，以及如何解决它们，可能看起来很不同。但我们在生活中娱乐自己的核心人类需求是相当相似的。（10:51）：我认为那些开发出真正好产品的公司，要么直观地，要么明确地花时间去真正理解这个旅程是什么，以及这些需求和痛点是什么，以及我们如何创造一个无缝的体验？

turns.speaker: Lenny

A quick follow-up question. So you have this tree with the outcome, say, get people to watch more Netflix. I imagine you recommend, max, three to five levers below that. Is that right? turns.zh: 我们会在节目笔记中链接到博客文章和一些示例，这样人们可以直观地看到这些内容，因为我知道我们试图用文字来描述它。一个快速的后续问题。那么你有这棵树，输出结果，比如让人们更多地观看Netflix。我想你建议，最多三到五个杠杆放在下面。对吗？然后其余的就放在其他地方？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah, that's a really good question. So at the top level, I tend to map those opportunities to steps in that experience map. So in that Netflix example, it'd be the trigger of I want to watch something, deciding what to watch, the viewing experience. I do find that, oh, is it Miller's magic number? The plus or minus seven rule is pretty good. I would say nine is probably a lot. So I would say maybe in that three to seven range. That's just because you could cognitively process your tree. (11:57): So the other thing that I get into is as you move vertically down the tree, your opportunities are getting smaller and smaller, which is really key to helping us unlock a continuous cadence. So if I start with that example of I can't decide what to watch, it's a really big hard evergreen problem. As long as Netflix is in business, they're probably going to have people focused on that problem. (12:16): But we can deconstruct it. Maybe I can't find something to watch because I don't know if this show's any good. Then we can learn about how do people evaluate shows. Maybe there's a small opportunity in there of who's the cast? It's one of the ways I evaluate a show. Now we're getting into an opportunity that we can actually solve. (12:33): So that's one of the other benefits. As we work our way down the tree, we get to smaller and smaller opportunities. We get to things that we can actually address. We're still contributing to that bigger, harder problem. And so, what it's allowing us to do is get this big picture view of where we could play, and then we can make more strategic decisions about where do we actually want to play. Then it's very customer-focused because it's really all about what's your need in this moment? How can I help satisfy that?
turns.zh:
是的，这确实是个很好的问题。首先，从最高层面来看，我倾向于将这些机会映射到体验地图中的各个步骤。比如拿Netflix举例，用户的需求可能分为三个阶段：首先是"我想看点东西"的触发点；其次是"决定看什么"的决策阶段；最后是观看体验阶段。我发现这里的关键点在于，用户对某个功能的认知负荷是否过高？比如Miller提到的"正负七条规则"就很有效，但九条可能就过多了。所以我认为理想的范围应该在三到七条之间。关键在于，随着用户向下探索体验树，机会会越来越少，而这正是帮助我们形成持续迭代节奏的关键。

（11:57）接下来要讨论的是，当我们沿着体验树向下深挖时，机会会逐渐缩小。这对我们解锁更复杂的难题至关重要。比如"我不知道该看什么"的难题，只要Netflix还在运营，这个问题就会一直存在。但我们可以拆解它：用户可能因为不确定剧集质量而犹豫不决。那么我们就可以研究人们如何评估剧集质量。可能其中一个小机会点是"演员阵容"——这正是我评估剧集质量的标准之一。这样我们就能找到切实可行的解决方案。

（12:33）这正是分解体验树的另一个好处：随着层级下移，机会会逐渐具体化，最终转化为可执行的行动。我们仍在为更宏大的难题贡献力量，而这让我们能全局把控可能的切入点，从而制定更具战略性的决策。这种方法以用户为核心，核心问题始终是：用户当下需要什么？如何满足他们的需求？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: If you want to reduce friction in your onboarding flow, then let me tell you about Stytch. That's Stytch with a Y. Stytch is on a mission to eliminate friction from the internet. They're starting by making user authentication and onboarding more seamless and more secure. They offer super flexible, out-of-the-box authentication solutions for companies of all size. From email magic links to SMS passcodes, one-tap social logins, to even biometrics Stytch is your all-in-one platform for authentication. (13:30): Stytch customers have been able to increase conversion by over 60% after spending just one day integrating. With their API and SDKs you can improve user conversion and retention and security all while saving valuable engineering time. Your engineers will come and thank you for using Stytch because Stytch keeps you from having to build authentication in-house, and the integration process is super fast and super smooth. To get $1,000 in free credits, just go to stytch.com, and that's Stytch with a Y, and sign up. Just mention that I sent you. (14:03): For PMs and just maybe founders that are listening and they're like, "This sounds really useful. I want to create my own little opportunity solution tree," I know this a big question, but how do you go about figuring out what goes into each of these steps, however briefly, you can give people some guidance?
turns.zh:
如果你想减少用户引导流程中的摩擦，那么让我向你介绍Stytch。Stytch的名字带Y。Stytch致力于消除互联网中的摩擦。他们的首个突破是让用户认证和引导流程更加无缝且安全。他们为各种规模的公司提供超灵活的开箱即用的认证解决方案。从邮箱魔法链接、短信验证码、一键社交登录到生物识别技术，Stytch是你的全能认证平台。

（13:30）Stytch客户在仅花一天时间集成后，转化率就能提升60%以上。通过他们的API和SDK，你可以提升用户转化率、留存率和安全性，同时节省宝贵的工程时间。你的工程师会感谢你使用Stytch，因为它省去了内部构建认证模块的麻烦，而且集成过程快速又顺畅。只需访问stytch.com（注意是带Y的Stytch）并注册，即可获得1000美元免费信用额度，并提及我是推荐的。

（14:03）对于正在听讲的产品经理和创业者，如果他们想创建自己的机会树，我知道这是一个大问题，但如何快速梳理每个步骤的要素呢？即使时间有限，能否给出一些指导？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah. So the reason why this is so hard is that ... I mean it sounds really simple, but here's why it's hard. Opportunities emerge from our customers' stories. I don't think most people, when they're interviewing, they collect stories. So if, Lenny, I was going to interview you about your Netflix experience, the vast majority of product teams are saying things like, "Hey, Lenny, what do you like to watch on Netflix? How do you decide what to watch?" We're asking these direct questions out of context. (14:43): The challenge with that is we know from human psychology and cognitive psychology that we're not very good at answering those questions out of context. Actually, that sounds weird. We're very good at answering them. Your brain will come up with a fast answer, but that answer doesn't necessarily reflect your behavior, and it misses context and nuance. (15:01): You can tell me, "I just like action movies. I always look for action movies." I can't visualize your experience. I don't know what your experience is watching action movies. I just collected a fact about you. But if I ask you, like, "Tell me about the last time you watched a movie," now I can collect things like where were you and who were you with and set the scene for me, and what happened first and how did you choose that? I'm going to get answers to all those direct questions, but it's grounded in this specific instance. It's going to be a lot more reliable. And I'm going to start to hear unmet needs, pain points, and desires. (15:36): The really powerful thing is I might hear needs that you're not even aware of. We're so used to everything being mediocre, we're not even aware of a lot of these needs that we have. But when we tell our stories, especially if you start to train your ear for this, you start to hear those needs. (15:54): So the first thing that makes this hard is you have to interview well. I think interviewing is a grossly underestimated skill. Grossly underestimated skill. So that's the first thing is that if you're not collecting rich stories in your interviews, it's going to be really hard to identify opportunities. (16:12): Then the second thing is that you have to be able to hear those opportunities. If you're still stuck with what's an opportunity versus what's a solution, it's tough. Then the third thing is this opportunity framing. I believe opportunity should be really specific. (16:27): A really great opportunity in the streaming space is it's hard to enter my password, select specific letters on the screen with the Apple TV remote. If anybody has had an Apple TV, especially the old remote, it's not a very precision device. Selecting those letters on the stupid onscreen keyboard is a horrible pain point. It comes up when we're entering our passwords, it comes up when we're searching for movie titles. That's a really specific opportunity. (16:53): The value of that is we can solve it. Whereas teams tend to want to frame opportunities as like, "I wish this was easier to use." Okay, well, we can spend our lives making this product easier to use. What are you solving for who? And so, we're skill stacking. Then we've got to interview well. We've got to be able to hear opportunities. We've got to be able to frame them well. Then in order to structure the opportunity space, we have to be able to come pull out this common experience map, structure across seemingly unique stories. (17:21): So there's a lot of skill involved. I wish I could just say, "Hey, Lenny. It's super easy. Everybody should do it. I think it's really powerful, and I've seen it be a game-changer for teams. It's hard. (17:32): I tell my teams when I teach it in class, I say, "Look, we're going to focus on structuring an opportunity space, and I'm probably going to make you think harder than you've ever had to think in your job," because we don't think that much at work. We go from meeting to meeting, we stay surface level a lot, and here I am coming in with this really hard critical thinking exercise. (17:53): But I've just seen from teams that are willing to put in that work, it really is a game-changer. You have a deeper understanding of what your customers need and you build better products.
turns.zh:
是的。所以这件事之所以这么难，是因为……我觉得听起来挺简单的，但实际原因在于机遇往往源自客户的故事。我觉得大多数人在面试时，收集的都是些零碎的信息。比如说，如果我要采访你关于Netflix的使用体验，大多数产品团队都会问你：“嘿，Lenny，你喜欢在Netflix上看什么？你是怎么决定看什么内容的？” 我们用这些脱离上下文的直接问题来提问。（14:43）问题在于，我们从人类心理学和认知心理学中知道，人们在脱离上下文的情况下很难准确回答这些问题。事实上，这听起来挺奇怪的。人们其实很擅长回答这些问题。但大脑给出的快速答案并不一定反映真实行为，而且会忽略背景和细节。（15:01）如果你直接问：“我喜欢动作片，总是找动作片看。” 我无法想象你的观影体验。我不知道你看动作片时的具体感受。我只收集到了一个关于你的事实。但如果你问：“能跟我讲讲你上次看电影的经历吗？” 这样我就能收集到当时的场景、同行伙伴，以及事件的先后顺序和选择过程。这些直接问题的答案才有真实依据，也更可靠。我还能从中捕捉到未被满足的需求、痛点和渴望。（15:36）最重要的是，我甚至可能听到你自己都没意识到的需求。我们太习惯于平庸的生活，许多潜在需求都被忽视了。但当我们讲述自己的故事时，尤其是当你逐渐培养这种倾听能力时，你就能捕捉到这些需求。（15:54）所以第一个挑战在于你得善于提问。我认为提问是一项被严重低估的技能。严重低估。所以如果你的采访中没有收集到丰富的故事，识别机遇就会变得异常困难。（16:12）第二个挑战在于你要能识别这些机遇。如果你还在纠结什么是机遇，什么是解决方案，那就太难了。第三个挑战是机遇的框定。我认为机遇应该非常具体。（16:27）在流媒体领域，一个很棒的机遇是，用户在Apple TV上输入密码时，用遥控器选择屏幕上的字母非常困难。如果有人用过Apple TV，尤其是老款遥控器，这设备的精度实在不高。在愚蠢的虚拟键盘上选择字母简直是痛苦至极。这种痛点在输入密码时出现，也在搜索电影片名时出现。这就是一个非常具体的机遇。（16:53）其价值在于我们可以解决它。而团队往往倾向于把机遇框定为“希望用起来更方便”。好吧，但我们可以把一生都花在让产品更方便上。但我们在为谁解决问题呢？所以我们需要掌握多种技能。首先要善于提问，善于识别机遇，善于框定机遇。然后，为了构建机遇空间，我们必须能够提取共通的经验地图，将看似独特的故事进行结构化。（17:21）所以这需要很高的技巧。我真希望能直接说：“嘿，Lenny。这超级简单。每个人都应该这么做。我觉得这真的很有效，我亲眼见证过。”
它能彻底改变团队的运作方式。但这并不容易。（17:32）我在课堂上讲授这项技能时会告诉学员：“听着，我们要专注于构建机会空间，而我可能会让你们进行比工作中更深入的思考。”因为职场中我们很少深入思考——我们总是在参加各种会议，停留在表层层面。而现在我要引入这种高强度的批判性思维训练。（17:53）但我观察到，那些愿意投入精力钻研的团队，确实因此受益匪浅。他们能更深刻地理解客户需求，从而打造出更优质的产品。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, thinking deeply.
turns.zh: 老兄，正在深思熟虑。

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No fun, but it's so important. I want to chat about interviewing and all the advice you have about just how to interview. But before we get to that, one last question around the opportunity solution work. So the whole idea is to think outcome-oriented. To your point, a lot of companies have product teams that are just like, "Build these things for us. Don't worry about why we're doing these." (18:24): If your company is of that ladder sort, more of a feature factory, can you use this framework to push the team and the company in a direction of thinking outcome-oriented, or is there a more direct approach to address that problem?
turns.zh: 虽然没意思，但这事儿太重要了。我想聊聊面试技巧，还有你对面试的所有建议。但在深入之前，最后再问个关于机会解决方案相关工作的题目。核心思路是以结果为导向。正如你所说，很多公司的产品团队都是那种“给我们开发这些功能，别管我们为什么要做这些”的状态。（18:24）：如果你的公司也是这种类型，更像是一个功能工厂，你能否利用这个框架推动团队和公司朝着结果导向的方向发展，还是说有更直接的方法来解决这个问题？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah. Okay. Let's talk about this based on the role. If you're an individual contributor and you're not at a 10-person company, I would say don't try to force the organizational change. Organizational change is such a hard and messy problem. I feel like what I would do in that situation is I would just change the way that I individually worked. (18:56): This is what I always did in every job. I mean I made a lot of mistakes trying to change the organization, but I also just carved out a way for me to work this way. I think we underestimate how much ability we have to do that. So even if you're being prescribed a fixed roadmap, you still can find customers to talk to. (19:14): I hear from people all the time say, "I'm not allowed to talk to customers." I go, "Okay, well, your company doesn't own you when you're not at work. I bet you know people like your customers. Why don't you just start there?" (19:24): So we overthink it. We think we have to go through these proper channels and we have to get permission from sales. A lot of us, especially if we work on a consumer product, just go find somebody that's like your user. But I've also seen instances in B2B environments, where like I worked with that team that worked on badges for healthcare, the badges that nurses and doctors use to unlock a workstation that they chart in. This team, for weeks, ran into problems finding a customer to talk to. (19:52): I just said, "Hey, do any of you know doctors or nurses in your personal network?" The product manager was like, "Yeah, I have two uncles that are doctors." "Huh. Maybe we could just start there." Go talk to somebody. (20:05): I think that even if you aren't being tasked with an outcome, if you do the work to understand these are the outcomes that matter to your business for your product, it's probably going to start with your business model, and then work to understand how the work that you're doing contributes to that. All those little teeny tiny decisions we make every day, even if you're being prescribed solutions, you'll make better decisions, because you have a fuller context of what your business needs. You have a fuller context of what your customer needs. (20:36): So I think for most of us, if you're in an individual contributor role, just focus on developing the habits yourself. I'm always amazed, I was always amazed at how much I could do by just ignoring everybody around me and how they were working and finding a way to do it.
turns.zh: 是啊，好的。那咱们就从角色出发来探讨这个问题。如果你是个普通员工，而且所在的公司规模不超过10人，我建议别试图强行推动组织变革。组织变革是个又难又混乱的课题。在这种情况下，我会先从自己个人的工作方式入手。（18:56）：这就是我在每个职位上都会做的事。说实话，我在试图改变组织架构时也犯过很多错误，但最终还是为自己开辟了一条路。我觉得我们低估了自己做到这点的能力。所以即便有人给你制定了固定的路线图，你仍然可以去找客户聊聊。（19:14）：我经常听到有人说：“我不被允许和客户交流。”我会说：“好吧，那你下班后公司可不会管你。我敢打赌你肯定认识一些和客户类似的人。你何不就从这儿入手呢？”（19:24）：我们想得太复杂了。我们总觉得必须走正规流程，必须获得销售部门的许可。我们很多人（尤其是做消费产品的人）只要找到和用户类似的人就行了。但我也见过B2B领域的例子，比如我曾和一个团队合作，为医疗保健行业开发徽章——护士和医生用来解锁工作站并记录病历的徽章。这个团队几周来都找不到能交流的客户。（19:52）：我只是说：“嘿，你们个人社交圈里有医生或护士吗？” 产品经理说：“有啊，我有两个叔叔是医生。” 我说：“嗯，或许我们可以从他们入手。”去找人聊聊。（20:05）：我觉得即便你没有被赋予明确的结果导向任务，只要你努力理解这些结果对你的业务和产品至关重要，这很可能始于你的商业模式，然后再去理解你正在做的工作如何为此做出贡献。我们每天做出的每一个微小决定，即便有人给你现成的解决方案，你也能做出更明智的决策，因为你能更全面地理解企业的需求和客户的需求。（20:36）：所以我认为对于大多数普通员工来说，只要专注于培养自己的习惯就行了。我一直很惊讶，靠着无视周围人的工作方式、找到自己的路径，我能做成那么多事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that because it lets you empower yourself and not wait for permission for excuses. This is always such a recipe for success for any role, especially PMs that are annoyed by how maybe their company works. (21:02): This is a really good segue to our second topic around continuous discovery. We've been touching on a lot of the elements of it, interviewing and understanding pain points and all that. And so, maybe just to set a little bit of foundation, what is continuous discovery? Your book is named after it. You, of course, is on this, which the general idea of continuous discovery.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这一点，因为它能让你赋予自己力量，不必等待许可或找借口。这对任何角色来说都是成功的秘诀，尤其是那些对公司运作方式感到不满的产品经理。（21:02）：这正好为我们引出第二个话题——持续探索。我们已经探讨了其中的许多要素，比如采访用户、理解痛点等等。所以，或许先来奠定一下基础，什么是持续探索？你的书就是以此命名的。当然，你对此深有体会，而持续探索的核心理念就是——

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah, let's just start at the beginning. So we often talk about discovery and contrast with delivery. Discovery is just used to describe the work we're doing to decide what to build. So everybody, every company is doing discovery. Everybody is making decisions about what to build. (21:37): We have a few trends that have been evolving very slowly over the last 20 years. One of which is we're recognizing that if we want to make good decisions about what to build, we probably should include the customer somewhere in that process. (21:49): So I teach a customer-centric view of discovery. Let's build in some feedback loops of are we making the right decisions, or are we making good decisions? Because there probably aren't right decisions here. (22:00): So then there's a second trend that we're seeing across the board, which is we're recognizing that digital products are never done. It's not like the Netflix team is going to show up to work one day and be like, "Hey, our product's good enough." We're always iterating, we're always improving. Customer needs are always evolving. There's always more we could do. (22:18): And so, we're seeing a shift from this project mindset that worked in a world where we were just trying to get products on a store shelf. We designed them, we built them, we manufactured them, we put them on the store shelf, we were done. We moved on to the next thing. (22:32): But with digital products, there's no done. So we're seeing this shift to more of a continuous mindset. We're continuously evolving our products, which means we're continuously making decisions about what to build and, therefore, I think we need to continuously include the customer in that process. So for me, I define continuous discovery as building in those continuous feedback loops.
turns.zh: 好的，让我们从头说起。我们常谈到探索与交付的对比。探索就是用来描述我们决定要构建什么的工作。因此，每个公司、每个人都在进行探索，都在决定要构建什么。（21:37）：过去20年间，有几个趋势在缓慢演变。其中之一是，我们意识到如果想做出正确的构建决策，或许应该在某个环节引入客户参与。（21:49）：所以我倡导以客户为中心的探索理念。我们要在过程中加入反馈回路：我们的决策是否正确？是否明智？因为这里不存在所谓的正确决策。（22:00）：接下来，我们观察到一个普遍趋势——数字产品永远没有完成的那一天。Netflix团队不会某天上班后宣布“我们的产品已经足够好了”。我们一直在迭代、改进，客户需求在不断变化，总有可以优化的地方。（22:18）：因此，我们正在从那种“只要把产品上架就万事大吉”的项目思维模式转变。数字产品没有终点，所以我们转向了持续改进的理念。我们持续迭代产品，这意味着我们需要持续决策要构建什么，因此，我认为我们需要持续让客户参与这个过程。对我来说，持续探索的定义就是在产品中嵌入持续的反馈回路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. That's such a simple, clear way of thinking about this because, yeah, broadly it's like a new term people have to get used to. I think you saw I made a call on Twitter for people to ask me to ask you questions about continuous discovery. And so, I'm going to try to get as many of those in there in this chat as I can. One actually was around what do you do when your leaders tell you there's no time for discovery?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这是一个简单明了的思考方式，因为，嗯，这个新术语确实需要人们慢慢适应。我记得你在Twitter上发起提问，邀请大家向你提问关于持续探索的问题。所以，我会尽可能在这次聊天中回答这些问题。其中一个问题是，当你的领导告诉你没有时间进行探索时，你会怎么做？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah, this is a tough one. I think this comes from old project-based research methods. So we don't most of the time have time to stop what we're doing and go do some research. I'm not pooh-poohing research. I mean I've worked as a user researcher. Research is critical. If we had the luxury of doing long longitudinal studies, we would probably build better products. (23:40): That's not our business environment. Our businesses are expecting us to deliver continuous value, so we need to look at how do we match that cadence. What I think is really nice about continuous discovery, you can do it in as little as an interview a week, on the interviewing side, on the discovering opportunity side. (23:58): Assumption testing. People always ask me, "How much time should I be spending on an assumption testing?" I don't know how to answer that question because for me, assumption testing and delivery are the same work. Assumption testing is the start of your delivery. I don't know where one starts and one ends, which is a little bit hard to conceptually work through, but maybe we can talk through an example. (24:20): So when somebody says, "I don't have time for discovery," I think what they're really saying is, "I don't have time for project-based research," and I agree with that. We don't have time for project-based research. So if I'm getting that pushback, I want to look for, okay, I definitely don't ... (24:33): Like people make this mistake of we shouldn't put something in our backlog that hasn't been properly discovered. It's not true. Everything in our backlog is a bet, everything. Whether we do discovery or not, everything is a bet. Discovery is helping us make a better bet. (24:52): Now sometimes in our organizations, we need to do a lot of discovery and make as good of a bet as we can. But there's other times we can make a risky bet. There's times in business where it makes sense to make a risky bet. If you work somewhere where all of your bets have been risky because you're doing zero discovery, the best way to kill any appetite for discovery is to say, "Let's stop making bets until we discover." No, don't do that. Keep making bets. In parallel, start doing some discovery so that eventually those bets get better. (25:29): I think the reason why people make this mistake is they think about it as phases. First I discover and then I deliver. No, you're always delivering and you're always discovering. The more you build this discovery habit, the better those bets are going to get with time. (25:44): So it's not that you do one first and then the other. It's you're always doing both. The benefit of always doing both is with time you make better bets.
turns.zh:
是啊，这确实是个难题。我觉得这源于传统的基于项目的研究方法。所以大多数时候，我们根本没时间停下手头工作，去专门做研究。我不是贬低研究的重要性——毕竟我自己也做过用户研究员，研究工作至关重要。要是我们有条件做长期纵向研究，或许能开发出更优质的产品，但现实毕竟不是那样。我们的业务环境要求我们持续创造价值，所以必须思考如何与这种节奏相匹配。  
（23:40）：这不是我们的商业环境。企业期待我们不断交付价值，所以得想办法如何与这种节奏同步。我觉得持续探索模式很棒——每周只需进行一次访谈，在访谈环节和发现机会环节就能完成探索。  
（23:58）：假设验证环节。总有人问我：“验证一个假设需要花多少时间？”我不知道该怎么回答，因为对我来说，验证假设和产品交付本质上是一体的。验证假设就是交付的开端。我分不清两者的界限，这在概念上确实有点难理解，不过或许我们可以通过一个例子来探讨。  
（24:20）：所以当有人说“我没时间做探索”时，我觉得他们真正的意思是“我没时间做基于项目的研究”，我对此深有同感。确实没时间做基于项目的研究。所以如果遇到这种反对意见，我会反问：“好吧，我确实没时间……” （24:33）：有些人会犯个错误，认为没经过充分探索就别放进产品待办列表。这是错误的。待办列表里的每一项都是个赌注，无论有没有做探索，每一项都是赌注。探索能帮我们下更好的赌注。  
（24:52）：有时在我们的组织里，需要做大量探索，尽可能下好赌注。但也有时候可以冒险一试。商业环境下，有些时候冒险赌注是合理的。如果你所在的公司因为零探索而一直冒险赌注，那么最有效的破局之道不是说“先别赌注，等我们探索清楚再说”。不，别这样。继续下赌注，同时开始探索，这样赌注才能逐渐优化。  
（25:29）：我觉得人们犯这个错误的原因是把探索和交付看成两个阶段。先探索再交付。不，你一直在交付，也一直在探索。越养成探索习惯，赌注就越稳妥。  
（25:44）：所以不是先做一项再做另一项。而是一直两手并进。两手并进的好处是，随着时间推移，你的赌注会越来越明智。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You said that you could do this with one meeting like an hour a week. I know you have a system that you recommend for people to make this automated so you're not just constantly pinging your customers, "Hey, can I chat with you this week?" Can you just share that?
turns.zh: 你说可以用每周一小时这样的频率来做探索。我知道你有个推荐的系统，可以自动化这个过程，这样就不用老是去烦客户：“嘿，这周能聊聊吗？”能分享一下那个系统吗？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah. So my book, Continuous Discovery Habits, I do share some of the most common ways to automate the recruiting process. So this idea came from ... I had just read Nudge by Thaler and Sunstein, when it came out a few years ago. They had this idea of when you're designing a choice architecture, how do you make it easier to adopt the behavior you want to see than to not adopt the behavior? (26:26): So I started thinking about this in the context of interviewing. I want to see product teams interview every week. So how do I make it easier for them to do that than to not do that? (26:35): Okay, well a lot of us have recurring meetings that we go to every week because they're on our calendar. So I just started to think about how do I make an interview a recurring meeting? Can I make it so that when you wake up on Monday morning, there's an interview on your calendar and you literally did nothing to get it there? (26:50): And so, there's a few ways to think about this. The most common strategy is to allow your customers to opt in while they're using your product or service. So just almost everybody's seen an NPS survey embedded in a product. That's pretty prevalent now. Same idea, but instead of saying, "Would you recommend our product or service to a friend or colleague?" it says, "Do you have 20 minutes to talk to us?" If they say yes, you send them some scheduling software, they pick a time on your calendar, and voila. You've got an interview scheduled. (27:18): You obviously can get more advanced. Where do you show it? Who do you show it to? How much do you tailor it? How do you position it? But the core idea is to let people opt in while you already have their attention. That works really well for consumers and B2B end users. (27:34): If you're trying to get in touch with buyers and decision-makers, same idea but use your internal teams that are already on the phone with those folks. So that salespeople, account managers, maybe support folks, they're literally on the phone with those people all day every day. So instead of using your product to recruit, you can use those teams to recruit. (27:54): What I do is I just have teams define a trigger every week, like, "Hey, this week we're looking to talk to somebody who's experiencing this need or pain point. If you happen to be on the phone with someone who's experiencing that, again, just go ahead and use scheduling software, put it on our calendar." The goal is for the product team to not be involved at all. They literally just have to show up and connect the interview.
turns.zh: 是的。我的书《持续探索习惯》（Continuous Discovery Habits）确实分享了一些自动化招聘流程的最常见方法。这一想法源于……几年前泰勒（Thaler）和森斯坦（Sunstein）的《助推》（Nudge）一书出版时。我当时刚读完这本书，他们提出了一个观点：当你设计选择架构时，如何让人们更容易采取你希望他们采取的行为，而不是不采取？（26:26）：所以我开始思考如何将这一理念应用于面试环节。我希望看到产品团队每周都进行面试。那么如何让他们更容易做到这一点，而不是不去做呢？（26:35）：好的，我们很多人每周都会参加重复的会议，因为这些会议被安排在日历上。于是我开始思考如何将面试变成重复的会议？能否让人们在周一早上醒来时，日历上就已经安排了一场面试，而他们无需为此做任何额外操作？（26:50）：实现这一目标有几种思路。最常见的策略是在用户使用产品或服务时让他们选择加入。比如现在很多产品中嵌入的NPS调查。这是个常见做法，但问题是用户被问到的是“你会向朋友或同事推荐我们的产品或服务吗？”而现在可以改为“你有20分钟时间和我们聊聊吗？”如果用户同意，你就给他们发送日程安排软件，让他们在日历上选择时间，然后面试就安排好了。（27:18）：当然还有更复杂的做法。比如在哪里展示？向谁展示？如何定制内容？如何定位？但核心思路是让人们在注意力被吸引时选择加入。这对消费者和B2B用户都非常有效。（27:34）：如果你试图联系买家和决策者，可以沿用同样的思路，但要利用内部团队，他们每天都在与这些人沟通。（27:54）：我的做法是让团队每周定义一个触发条件，比如“本周我们想和有这种需求或痛点的人聊聊。如果你正好在和有这种需求的人通话，再次提醒他们使用日程安排软件，把会议安排到我们的日历上。”目标是让产品团队完全不参与其中，他们只需按部就班地安排面试即可。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's amazing. Are there tools that you recommend that are just plug and play that make this easy? I know Calendly is probably a part of this.
turns.zh: 太棒了。有没有现成可用的工具能轻松实现这一点？我知道Calendly可能就是其中之一。

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: There are so many. So even on the scheduling side, I think Calendly innovated in that space, but there's so many fast followers. I think Outlook does this now. I think Google has a tool that does this now. I think even Salesforce has a tool that does this now. So if you're sales team is scheduling through Salesforce. Then on the intercept side, like how are you asking those? We have survey tools. (28:45): Qualaroo, I think, innovated in this space. Then I think Ethnio is a fast follower. But Intercom does this, Usabilla does this, Chameleon does this. Hotjar might even do this. We have so many user research tools that they're all now enabling this type of thing.
turns.zh: 有很多工具。比如在日程安排方面，我认为Calendly在这一领域有所创新，但有很多跟风者。Outlook现在也支持这项功能，Google也有相关工具，甚至Salesforce也推出了类似工具。所以如果你的销售团队通过Salesforce安排日程，那么在拦截环节，比如如何询问这些信息？我们有调查工具。（28:45）：我认为Qualaroo在这方面有所创新。Ethnio也是跟风者。Intercom、Usabilla、Chameleon也支持这项功能。Hotjar可能也会提供相关功能。现在有很多用户研究工具，都支持这类功能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. For when you're actually doing the interviewing, we had a couple of questions from some Teresa fans. One is when you know what the solution should be, how do you stay disciplined and keep an open mind and keep searching for maybe something even better?
turns.zh: 太棒了。说到你实际进行面试时，我们收到了一些特蕾莎粉丝的问题。其中一个是，当你知道应该采用什么解决方案时，如何保持纪律性，同时保持开放的心态，继续寻找可能更优的方案？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah. First of all, you don't always have to do that. Not all solutions need a lot of discovery. That's a common misunderstanding, I think. I think we need to do really robust, good discovery on the things that are part of our core product experience or going to be differentiators. We don't really have to do really amazing core discovery on the forgot password flow if it's working fine and you're not hearing about it as a pain point. (29:42): Now to be fair, Slack with their magic link, did a cool thing with the forgot password flow. That was a nice innovative thing that I think moved the industry forward. So if you want to do discovery on that, great, but you probably don't have to. So I think the first thing to assess is we're making a bet. How much risk is involved in this bet and how much of that risk do we need to mitigate? (30:06): Now most companies think there's no risk in any bets and they do zero discovery. If you're not instrumenting your product and actually measuring the impact of those solutions, you may not be catching that there actually was a lot of risk. So I think you do need to instrument your product. You do need to measure the impact of everything that you release so you can start honing your judgment on where is there risk in ideas. (30:29): When you're new to discovery, I recommend you overindex on doing a little too much discovery so that you start honing your judgment of that risk. But if you're working on an opportunity that's really core to your product functionality, it is a differentiator, it's where you want to make sure you have a really robust, good solution, I think the best way to guard against what you think is the obvious solution is to work with multiple solutions for the same opportunity. (30:53): Compare and contrast. We already know this intuitively. When you're looking for a place to live, you don't look at one apartment or house. You look at multiple, you compare and contrast. When you're looking for a job, you don't talk to one company. We know if we want to make good decisions, we need options and we need to evaluate the pros and cons of each. The same is true in the product world. (31:13): So if you're feeling like this needs to be a really good solution and we're having some challenges, we're overcommitting to one, that's when you need to increase your options.
turns.zh: 是的。首先，你并非总是需要这样做。并非所有解决方案都需要大量探索。我认为这是一个常见的误解。我们确实需要对构成核心产品体验或具有差异化特性的内容进行非常扎实、优质的探索。但对于忘记密码流程，如果它运行良好，且用户没有将其视为痛点，那么你没必要在这上面进行惊艳的核心探索。（29:42）：公平地说，Slack凭借其魔法链接，在忘记密码流程方面做得很棒。这是一个很好的创新举措，推动了行业进步。所以如果你想对此进行探索，那很好，但你可能没必要这样做。因此，我认为首先要评估的是我们在下注。这种下注涉及多大的风险，我们需要减轻多少风险？（30:06）：现在大多数公司认为任何下注都没有风险，他们根本不进行探索。如果你不为产品配备监控工具，也不实际衡量这些解决方案的影响，你可能就意识不到实际上存在着巨大的风险。所以我认为你确实需要为产品配备监控工具。你需要衡量你发布的每一项内容的影响，这样你才能开始磨练自己对风险所在的判断。（30:29）：当你刚开始进行探索时，我建议你过度投入进行一点探索，这样你就能开始磨练自己对风险的判断。但如果你正在处理对产品功能至关重要的机会，它是差异化因素，是你希望确保拥有一个非常扎实、优质解决方案的地方，我认为防范你认为显而易见的解决方案的最佳方法是针对同一机会探索多种解决方案。（30:53）：比较和对比。我们直观地知道这一点。当你寻找住所时，你不会只看一套公寓或一栋房子，而是会看多个并进行比较和对比。当你找工作时，你不会只与一家公司沟通。我们知道，如果我们想做出好的决策，我们需要选项，需要评估每个选项的利弊。在产品领域也是如此。（31:13）：所以如果你觉得这需要一个非常好的解决方案，而我们遇到了挑战，我们过度投入于一个解决方案，那就是你需要增加选项的时候了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'd love your insight on, as a PM, how much ... In theory, you should be a little bit unbiased and giving people a chance to change your mind and come up with ideas that maybe you disagree with. On the other hand, as a PM, you always have opinions about what the right answer is. Just like in the PM function, do you have a perspective on how much more, say, a PM should have maybe over what ends up being decided?
turns.zh: 我想听听你作为产品经理的见解。从理论上讲，你应该保持一定的公正性，让人们有机会改变你的想法，提出你可能不认同的观点。另一方面，作为产品经理，你总是对正确的答案有自己的看法。正如产品经理职位所要求的，你对产品经理应该在最终决策中拥有多少自主权有何看法？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah, this is a tough question. I mean there's such strong opinions about this. I mean I see analogies of the product manager is the decider and they're the CEO of the product. I think this is coming from toxic business culture personally. Business has taught us we all play a role. We have our functional silos. I have territory, you have territory, and we're going to play the internal office politics game. I need to defend my territory and you need to defend your territory. (32:13): The outcome is that we don't really collaborate. When we don't collaborate, I don't think we build very good products. So if we just go back to real life and when you're hanging out with friends and you're trying to accomplish something, the example I gave is when you're a little kid and you're playing, you don't like to first stop and say, "What's my role? What's your role?" I guess it's just not how humans interact. We all collaborate and we all do it intuitively. Business has taught us otherwise. (32:40): I'm going to forget the researcher, but there's a really cool ... The marshmallow test experiment. Are you familiar with this? Where teams are given spaghetti sticks and some tape and some string and a marshmallow. They're told to build a structure to get the marshmallow as high as possible. (32:56): A study's been done so many times. It's been replicated a million times with lots of different groups. It's a really cool story because kindergartners outperform almost every adult group, including MBA students. It's really telling. Why is this? (33:10): Kindergartners just start doing. They don't worry about their rules. They don't worry about who's in charge. They just brute force trial and error. What do MBA students do? There's posturing, like who has power and who's the decision-maker and who's right? We need a plan and we need to have a strategy. They spend the whole time negotiating this political social space instead of just doing. I really think we've got to learn how to get back to just doing. (33:37): And so, people think that I'm like Pollyanna naive about this, but I've worked on teams that work this way and I've coached teams that work this way where the trio really does decide. So the trio is the product manager, the designer, and the software engineer. If you've never worked in a well-functioning trio, this breaks people's brains, because they say, "Well, what are we going to do when we disagree?" You're going to find an option where you don't disagree. (34:00): The thing is if you only worked on a siloed dysfunctional team, that sounds like a nightmare. But if you've worked on a well-functioning team that's doing discovery well together, you're working from a shared understanding. So your disagreements right away are going to go way down because you're working from a shared understanding, and when you disagree, you recognize, okay, we don't agree, we don't have the best option yet. You keep looking for that better option. (34:26): What's hard about talking about this is I fully understand probably 98% of the industry has never worked on a well-functioning product trio, and this idea sounds crazy. But I've also seen it in practice over and over again on really good teams, and there's something magical about it. So I'm going to keep promoting it and I'm going to hope that eventually we get from 2% to 3%. That'll be my little debt I put in the universe.
turns.zh: 是啊，这真是个难题。我是说大家对这个问题意见分歧很大。比如有人把产品经理比作决策者、产品CEO之类的。我觉得这源于有毒的商业文化。商业教会我们每个人都扮演特定角色，存在职能隔阂——我管我的地盘，你管你的地盘，然后就是内部勾心斗角的政治游戏。我需要捍卫自己的地盘，你也需要捍卫你的地盘。（32:13）结果就是大家根本无法有效协作。缺乏协作能力，就很难做出优质产品。退回到现实生活，当你和朋友一起做事时，比如小时候玩耍时，大家不会先停下来问“我该扮演什么角色？你该扮演什么角色？”这根本不符合人类的交际方式。我们天生就会协作，凭直觉行动。但商业却教会了我们相反的做法。（32:40）我忘了提研究者，但有个超酷的实验叫“棉花糖测试”。你知道吗？就是给团队提供意大利面条、胶带和绳子，要求他们用这些材料搭建结构，让棉花糖尽可能高高挂起。（32:56）这个实验做过无数次，在不同群体中重复验证。最震惊的是幼儿园小朋友的表现几乎碾压所有成年组，包括MBA学生。这很能说明问题。为什么呢？（33:10）小朋友直接动手，不在乎规则，不在乎谁说了算。他们靠蛮力不断尝试。而MBA学生呢？他们在乎职位、权力归属、谁对谁错？他们总在谈判权力空间，却不行动。我认为我们需要回归行动本质。（33:37）有人觉得我天真乐观，但我确实在高效运作的团队中实践过三人决策模式。三人组包括产品经理、设计师和软件工程师。没体验过这样的团队的人会觉得不可思议，但在协作良好的团队里，大家从共识出发，分歧瞬间消失。（34:00）如果你只在隔绝的混乱团队工作过，那简直是噩梦。但在高效探索的团队里，大家基于共识协作，分歧自然减少，因为共识让大家意识到“我们意见不合，但还没找到最佳方案”，然后继续寻找更优解。（34:26）要解释这个观点很难，因为98%的从业者从未体验过高效的三人团队，这个理念听起来很疯狂。但我在优秀团队中见证过其魔力。我会继续推广，希望能从2%提升到3%。这就是我对世界的小小贡献。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I was just going to say that you're helping make that change and I'm excited for that to be the way that people operate. And so, maybe one takeaway is if that's something that you're spending a lot of time on and it's causing you a lot of stress, it probably means you're working at a company or on a team that maybe isn't optimal.
turns.zh: 是啊。我正想说，你正在助力推动这种变革，我对人们能以这种方式开展工作感到兴奋。所以，也许有一点启示是，如果你花大量时间在某件事上却倍感压力，这很可能意味着你所在的公司或团队的运作方式并不理想。

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: I don't mean that to say there's something wrong with you or your teammates. This is a symptom of business culture. It's how we've been taught to work. So we have to unlearn that. We have to learn new ways of working. We do this in our courses. We force people to work in teams in our courses, and some people really hate it. But I think learning to work well in a team, especially when there's different perspectives and you disagree and how do you reconcile that, is a really important part of product work.
turns.zh: 我这么说不是说你或你的团队有问题。这是商业文化的表征，也是我们被教导的工作方式。所以我们必须摒弃这些旧习，学习新的工作方式。我们在课程中就致力于此。我们强制学员在团队中协作，有些人对此深恶痛绝。但我认为学会团队协作至关重要，尤其是当存在不同观点、意见不合时，如何化解分歧，这正是产品工作中最重要的环节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Going back to discovery and interviewing, I definitely wanted to ask you what are, I don't know, two or three tips and best practices for interviewing/what are two or three things people usually do wrong that they should try to avoid?
turns.zh: 太棒了。回到探索和面试环节，我特别想问你，有没有什么面试技巧或最佳实践？或者人们常犯的错误有哪些需要避免的？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah. The first one is the questions they're asking. So many people write these who why, how, 50-question long interview protocols. It leads to a cadence of the interview that is not a natural conversation. So I think the first thing to remember is that you're just talking to a human. (36:06): I actually tell people if your interview feels like you're having a beer with a buddy, that's a good sign. It should be that casual and that conversational. But we're not going to get there if I pepper you with 50 questions. We're going to get there by I'm going to collect your story. I'm going to be really curious. I might still have to pepper you with 50 questions to get your story, because there's this conversational norm of I say something, you say something. So I've got to teach you that I want your whole story and help you open up. (36:36): So that's one piece of it. It's just the cadence of the conversation really should feel like a natural conversation. Then the second piece of it is how do we do that? What's the skill? How do we elicit that story? (36:46): I teach in our interviewing class, you really don't have to think about what to ask. You could run an entire interview by asking them one question. In fact, let's role play this a little bit. Lenny, tell me about the last time you watched something on a streaming entertainment service.
turns.zh: 是的。首先是提问方式。太多人写那些长达50个问题的结构化面试协议，面试过程完全没有自然对话的感觉。所以我认为首要记住的是，你只是在和一个人交谈。（36:06）：我常对人说，如果面试过程让你感觉像是在和朋友喝啤酒，那就是个好兆头。它应该轻松随意。但如果你用50个问题狂轰滥炸，就达不到这种效果了。我们要通过收集对方的故事来获取信息，可能还需要用50个问题来引导，但前提是得让对话自然流畅，符合交谈的规范——我说一句，你回应一句。所以我得教会你，我需要听到整个故事，帮助你敞开心扉。（36:36）：这就是第一点。对话的节奏必须自然。第二点是如何做到这一点？需要什么技巧？如何挖掘出这些故事？（36:46）：在我们的面试课程中，我教导学员其实无需刻意构思问题。你完全可以通过一个问题贯穿整个面试。事实上，我们来角色扮演一下。莱尼，讲讲你上次在流媒体娱乐平台上看节目的情况。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just last night I was watching Obi-Wan Kenobi on Disney+.
turns.zh: 就在昨晚，我在Disney+上看《欧比旺·肯诺比》。

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Okay. Yeah. Great. Okay, so it was last night. Set the scene for me. Where were you?
turns.zh: 好的。是啊，很棒。好的，昨晚的情况是这样的。请给我描述一下当时的场景。你在哪里？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was at home on my couch, just lounging.
turns.zh: 我在家，躺在沙发上休息。

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Okay. Tell me about the moment where you decided you wanted to watch something.
turns.zh: 好的。讲讲你决定要看节目的那个瞬间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was 8:00 and I'm like, "It's time to watch something."
turns.zh: 晚上8点，我心想：“是时候看点什么了。”

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Okay. Is that part of your normal routine?
turns.zh: 好的。这是你日常的习惯吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, in the evenings. It's a good way to unwind and let my brain relax a little bit. Okay,
turns.zh: 是的，晚上经常这样。这是放松大脑的好方法。好的，

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Okay. So you're sitting on the couch, you decided it's time to watch something. What did you do next?
turns.zh: 好的。那么你坐在沙发上，决定要看节目了。接下来你做了什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Turned on the TV, went to Netflix, didn't find anything. Went to Prime, didn't find anything. I'm like, "Oh yeah, Obi-Wan. Let's check that out."
turns.zh: 打开电视，切换到Netflix，一无所获。再去Prime，也没找到合适的内容。我当时就想：“哦，对了，《欧比旺·肯诺比》！看看这个吧。”

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Okay. So I literally could continue this entire interview by just saying, "Oh, you opened Netflix. What happened next? Oh, you didn't find anything. How come?" All I have to do is just be curious about your experience. What I'm doing with my questions is just helping you tell the timeline. (37:59): Set the scene. I'm situating you back in that moment. Let's remember what you actually did. It was after dinner. You were sitting on the couch. What happened next? I can do that over and over again. (38:09): And so, one of the reasons why we get bad at interviewing, we're so worried about asking the next question, we stop listening to the interviewee. We just missed everything we were told. We missed those moments of like, "Oh, there is some friction. You couldn't find something to watch. Tell me about that. What did you consider on Netflix? Let's dig into that." (38:27): If I work on a team that's trying to help you find something to watch, that's a gold mine. You just told me you went on Netflix, you went on Prime. What were you looking at and what didn't resonate? Is it because you'd watched everything? Is it because it just didn't match your profile? There's so much to explore there. (38:44): But what I see most teams do is they stay really shallow. "Oh, okay. So you watched Obi-Wan on Prime. Great. Tell me another story." We just lost all the value. (38:57): And so, some of it is just slowing down and almost being a five-year-old. You really, instead of saying, "Why? Why? Why?" you can say, "What happened next? What happened next?" (39:08): Now there's this technique of summarize what you heard, show that you're listening to them, bring them back to the moment where you want a little more detail. But, yeah, it's a game-changer. What happens when you collect stories is you hear about things you would've never thought to ask about.
turns.zh:
好的。所以我完全可以把整个采访继续下去，只要一直问：“哦，你打开了Netflix。接下来发生了什么？哦，你什么都没找到。为什么呢？”我只需要对你的经历保持好奇。我的提问就是在帮助你理清时间线。
（37:59）：先设定场景。我要把你带回当时的状态。让我们回想一下你实际做了什么。晚饭后你坐在沙发上。接下来发生了什么？我可以反复这样做。
（38:09）：所以，我们之所以不擅长采访，就是因为太担心下一个问题会问什么，结果没听清对方在说什么。我们错过了所有关键信息。比如，“哦，找不到想看的内容。能具体说说你找了哪些内容吗？”或者“你觉得Netflix上的内容不符合你的口味吗？”这些都是值得深挖的地方。
（38:44）：但我看到大多数团队做得太表面了。“哦，好吧，你在Prime上看了《欧比旺·肯诺比》。不错，再讲个故事吧。”这样就完全失去了价值。
（38:57）：所以，有时候你需要放慢节奏，像个五岁孩子一样。不要总是追问“为什么？”，而是要说“接下来发生了什么？接下来发生了什么？”这样既能让对方保持专注，又能把话题引回到你想了解更多细节的时刻。这种技巧真的很有效。当你收集了这些故事后，你会发现很多你之前从未想到过要去询问的内容。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's also really fun to share because I'm like, "Oh, this is fun," just talking about what I do.
turns.zh: 分享这些经历也很有趣，因为我会想：“哦，这真有趣。”谈论我的工作真的很有意思。

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: I love that you just said that, because people worry. How many times have you heard somebody say, like ... You asked the sales rep, "Hey, can I talk to your customer?" and they're like, "I don't want to ask them a favor." It turns out if you collect stories in your interviews, customers love it. Most of the time, in fact the sign that you ran a good interview, is your customer is going to say, "Wow. When can we do this again?"
turns.zh: 我很高兴你提到这一点，因为人们总是担心。你听过多少次有人说：你去问销售代表，“能让我和你的客户聊聊吗？”对方却说：“我不想麻烦他们。”结果发现，如果你在采访中收集这些故事，客户会很喜欢。大多数情况下，如果你成功地进行了采访，客户会说：“哇，我们什么时候能再聊聊？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I love that. The other piece of this that you haven't mentioned is there's a lot of focus on what you've done, not on what you would do or you could do. I imagine that's an important part of this.
turns.zh: 哇。我太喜欢这个了。你没提到的一个关键点是，人们往往只关注自己做过什么，而忽略了自己可能做什么或应该做什么。我想这也是很重要的一点。

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Product people are in the business of changing behavior, understanding and changing behavior. I think that's a really big mistake that teams make is, both in their prototype tests and in their interviews, they focus on what people would do, on what people think, on why they think they do something. It's all really unreliable. It's a garbage in, garbage out situation. The real measure is tell me about your behavior. What did you actually do? We have to help people do that.
turns.zh: 产品人员的职责是改变用户行为，理解并改变他们的行为。我认为团队常犯的一个大错误是，无论是在原型测试还是采访中，他们都只关注人们可能会做什么、会怎么想、为什么会这么想。这都是不可靠的。这就是信息输入和输出的循环。真正重要的衡量标准是让我了解你的行为。你实际做了什么？我们需要帮助人们做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something else someone asked that I really wanted to cover is how does this process change as your company grows from early stage to later stage?
turns.zh: 有人问的一个问题，我特别想讲讲的，就是随着公司从早期阶段发展到后期阶段，这个过程会如何变化？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah. In an ideal world, it doesn't change because here's why. If I have a trio and they have an outcome and they're empowered to reach that outcome, and they're interviewing every week and their assumption testing to evaluate solutions, and they're finding things to build and they're driving their outcome, that's a really successful team. They could do that in a three-person company or they could do that in a hundred thousand-person company. (40:58): The primary difference is in a three-person company, there's no adjacent teams. In a hundred thousand-person company, there's a lot of adjacent teams. And so, you probably have some dependencies to manage. But you still should start with an outcome, be empowered to go after it, be empowered to come up with your own solutions. (41:17): What's going to be different in that a hundred thousand-person company is you probably have design patterns and libraries you got to rely on for a coherent user experience. You probably have another team that's working adjacent to you that you need to share your discovery work and be aware of what they're working on, because you do need to build a coherent product. (41:34): And so, as our companies get bigger, we have a lot of that lateral collaboration we have to do to make sure we're still building a coherent product. But I think the fundamental base unit stays the same.
turns.zh: 是啊。在理想情况下，这个过程不会改变，原因如下。如果我有一个三人团队，他们有明确的目标，有权力去实现这个目标，每周进行采访和假设测试来评估解决方案，找到可开发的方向并推动目标达成，这就是一个非常成功的团队。无论是在三人公司还是十万人公司，他们都能做到这些。（40:58）：主要的区别在于，三人公司没有相邻的团队；十万人公司则有很多相邻的团队。因此，你可能需要管理一些依赖关系。但你仍然应该从一个目标开始，赋予团队追逐目标的权力，允许他们自主提出解决方案。（41:17）：在十万人公司，情况会有所不同——你可能需要依赖设计模式和库来确保用户体验的一致性。你可能需要与相邻团队共享发现成果，并留意他们的工作进展，因为你确实需要构建一个连贯的产品。（41:34）：随着公司规模扩大，为了确保产品连贯性，我们必须开展大量横向协作。但我认为基本的核心单元始终不变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that I've seen happen with larger companies, especially as companies grow, is a little bit of cynicism of user research, specifically how few people you talk to and how that leads to you making a decision. How do you respond to those kinds of concerns?
turns.zh: 我观察到大公司，特别是随着公司发展壮大，用户研究会遭遇一些质疑，比如只访谈少数用户就做出决策的可靠性如何。对此你如何回应？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: I love this. I don't know why product teams suddenly are held to a standard that nobody else is held to. When somebody says something like, "Why is it reliable to make a decision based on one interview?" I just flip the question around. Tell me about the decisions you made last week. How many customers did you talk to? What data did you use? (42:20): Every human in business is making decisions with zero data. So I'm going to go with one is better than zero. That's a little bit of a flippant answer, but it's true. (42:32): Here's what's happening when that question comes up. I have an opinion that's different than yours. I don't like your conclusion so I'm going to nitpick it. In the product world, unfortunately, everybody in business has an opinion about what we should be building. And so, that's how we face that and we get held to this standard. (42:52): I have a real reason why we can make decisions based on small data. We're in the business of changing behavior, not seeking new knowledge. We have really good feedback loops. And so, we can make decisions based on small experiments because we're going to continue to get bigger feedback loops and more reliable data over time. Especially as we deliver and we do live production prototyping, we actually can get large-scale data. I don't want to start there because we're never going to ship anything. (43:17): So there is legitimately a valid reason why we can work on small data, but it's an unfair question, because we're not holding anybody else in business to that standard.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个问题。不明白为什么产品团队突然要遵循一个别人都不需要遵循的标准。当有人问“仅凭一次访谈就能做出可靠决策吗？”时，我会反问：“上周你做了哪些决策？访谈了多少用户？用了哪些数据？”（42:20）：商界里的每个人都在基于零数据做决策。所以我宁愿选择“有总比没有好”。这听起来有点不客气，但确实如此。（42:32）：当这种质疑出现时，通常是对方不同意我的观点，不喜欢我的结论，于是开始吹毛求疵。在产品领域，不幸的是，所有人都对我们应该开发的产品品头论足。这就是我们面临这种标准的原因。（42:52）：我确实有理由基于少量数据做决策。我们从事的是改变用户行为的业务，不是探索新知识。我们有非常好的反馈循环。因此，我们可以基于小规模实验做决策，因为随着时间推移，我们会获得更大的反馈循环和更可靠的数据。特别是当我们上线产品并进行实时原型测试时，我们就能获得大规模数据了。但我不想从这点开始讲，因为我们永远无法真正将任何产品推向市场。（43:17）：所以基于少量数据工作的确有合理性，但这是一个不公平的问题，因为我们没有让商界其他人遵循这个标准。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Along those lines, when does it make sense to run an experiment versus rely on user research? Do you have a mental model for how you think about that?
turns.zh: 沿着这个思路，当何时应该开展实验而非依赖用户研究呢？对于这个问题，你是否有自己的思维模型？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Our language around this is terrible. It's so ambiguous. What's an experiment? What's user research? I would say experiments are user research. I'm trying to just dramatically simplify this. (43:43): I think from a discovery standpoint, we have two core activities: qualitative interviewing and assumption testing. And so, with qualitative interviewing, we're trying to learn about the opportunity space. Where do we see unmet needs, pain points, and desires? Interviewing is not the only way to identify opportunities. Observations are actually a better way. I focus on interviewing because it's something we can do sustainably week over week. Most teams don't have the ability to observe their customers every week. (44:11): On the assumption testing side, for me, anything that helps us evaluate a solution where we're starting with a very specific assumption is an assumption test. So we have experiments that I actually don't even think we should be running, because they're testing the whole idea before we have any idea if that idea has a strong foundation. They're taking too long. They cost too much money. They're taking too much time. So how do I break this down? (44:37): The first thing is we have to learn how to take an idea and break it into its underlying assumptions. We have to learn how to prioritize those assumptions. Then we have to learn how to run tests that are small enough that they're just testing that assumption. (44:51): This is all critical because it's what makes continuous discovery sustainable. I tell people to work with three ideas at once, and teams are struggling to test even a single idea. So how's that sustainable? Well, that team that's struggling to test a single idea is still stuck in project-based research world. They're running experiments that take weeks to get results. (45:13): Whereas when I talk about assumption testing, I'm working with a team that's running half a dozen to a dozen assumption tests in one week, and those assumptions span three ideas. At the end of the week, they can start to compare and contrast those solutions. So we've got to shift our methods. Continuous discovery is sustainable if we change our behavior, if we change our habits.
turns.zh: 我们对此的表述实在糟糕。太模糊了。什么是实验？什么是用户研究？我会说实验就是用户研究。我想把这件事简单化。（43:43）：从发现阶段来看，我们有两个核心活动：定性访谈和假设验证。通过定性访谈，我们试图了解机会空间。哪里存在未满足的需求、痛点和愿望？访谈并非识别机会的唯一方式。观察实际上是更好的途径。我专注于访谈，因为这是我们每周都能持续开展的工作。大多数团队没有能力每周观察客户。（44:11）：在假设验证方面，对我来说，任何帮助我们评估基于特定假设的解决方案的活动都属于假设验证。因此，有些实验我认为根本不该开展，因为它们在我们尚未确认该想法是否有坚实基础之前就开始测试整个概念。它们耗时太久、花费太多，效率太低。那么如何拆解这个问题呢？（44:37）：首先，我们要学会如何将一个想法分解成其底层假设。我们要学会如何对这些假设进行优先排序。然后，我们要学会如何运行规模足够小的测试，这些测试仅针对某个假设进行验证。（44:51）：这一切至关重要，因为它能让持续发现模式得以持续。我告诉人们同时处理三个想法，但很多团队连单个想法的测试都做不到。那怎么能持续呢？嗯，那个连单个想法测试都困难的团队，仍然停留在基于项目的研究世界里。他们开展的实验需要数周才能得出结果。（45:13）：而当我谈到假设验证时，我合作的团队一周会进行六到十次假设验证，这些假设横跨三个想法。周末结束时，他们就能开始比较和对比这些解决方案了。所以我们必须改变方法。只要我们改变行为、改变习惯，持续发现就能持续下去。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For folks that want to learn more about assumption testing, continuous discovery, all the things that you've been chatting about, where can they find you online and find these courses online?
turns.zh: 对于想了解更多假设验证、持续发现以及您所谈论的所有内容的人，他们可以在哪里在线找到您和相关课程？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Yeah. So first I'll mention the book, Continuous Discovery Habits. It's available at bookstores around the world. It's in EPUB, paperback, and Audible. Then I do blog about all of this at producttalk.org and our courses are at learn.producttalk.org.
turns.zh: 是的。首先，我要提到《持续发现习惯》这本书。全球书店均有销售，有EPUB、纸质版和Audible版本。然后我在producttalk.org上写博客，讨论所有这些内容，我们的课程在learn.producttalk.org上。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. I also love to ask guests, how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我还想问嘉宾，听众如何能为您提供帮助？

turns.speaker: Teresa Torres
turns.en: Since the book has come out, the reaction has been unbelievably amazing and a lot of fun. And I'm a little bit overwhelmed by people in the industry who have never been exposed to this way of working having a lot of skepticism that it's possible. (46:17): So here's how listeners can be helpful. I didn't make up this way of working. This way of working evolved from teams figuring this out.
